newsitem.title: USA: Opponents of Pacific Pipeline LA line to battle on.
newsitem.headline: Opponents of Pacific Pipeline LA line to battle on.

text.p: Opponents of a proposed oil pipeline through northeast Los Angeles will renew their fight to stop its construction later this month, despite losing earlier legal battles, a city official said.
The Pacific Pipeline, scheduled for construction later this year, would extend an existing line that runs from fields offshore Santa Barbara, California, to the state's San Joaquin Valley.

"There are still some pending legal actions," said Woody Hastings, an aide to Los Angeles City Councilman Richard Alarcon. "We feel we've got good reason for opposing the pipeline. We stand by those reasons."
The proposed 132-mile leg would carry 130,000 barrels-per-day of San Joaquin Valley and offshore crudes to refineries south of the city.
Alarcon and other opponents say the line could endanger people living in the heavily populated valley Northeast of Los Angeles, a city prone to earthquakes.
They plan to challenge Pacific on grounds it violates the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and will bring their case to a hearing on February 24th in state superior court.
They may also appeal a recent court ruling that gives pipeline builders the right to construct on property owned by the City of Los Angeles, Hastings said.
Oppponents lost an earlier challenge against the U.S. Forest Service, which gave Pacific permission to build on Federal property north of the city.
Meanwhile, pipeline officials plan to begin construction as soon as possible in order to complete the line in 1997.
"It's a nine to 12 month construction period. We want to get it going," said Chuck McClean, spokesman for Pacific Pipeline Inc, which is owned by Colorado-based Anshutz Corp.
The pipeline company has filed a motion to throw out the environmental charges.
"We don't consider it a serious appeal," McClean said, adding his company's motion could be heard within two weeks.

But opponents say earlier appeals did not fully consider alternative routes through existing pipelines, such as Atlantic Richfield Co.'s Line 90 and an old fuel oil line owned by Edison International.
Arguing the Pacific line would " disproportionately impact on communities of color" Alarcon's staff contends the alternative routes need more consideration.
But Pacific says future challenges cannot halt their construction plans.
"None of the legal stuff will now prevent us from moving ahead," McClean said.
Several oil companies, including Texaco and Chevron backed Pacific, saying it is technically and environmentally superior to other means of transport. Pacific also claims it is significantly cheaper.
"It seems to me Pacific has the advantage of shipper support," said John Vautrain, an analyst for Purvin & Getz Inc. in Long Beach, California.
